overview:
A line of rulers based in the Ganges plain — probably in what is now eastern Uttar Pradesh or Bihar, though even their homeland is argued over — rose from local prominence to imperial scale within about three generations. A marriage alliance with the old Licchavi clan gave Chandragupta I the standing to call himself "great king of kings," and an era count beginning around 319 CE marks the moment the dynasty began to date the world by itself. His successor Samudragupta (roughly the middle third of the fourth century; scholars place the reign anywhere from the 330s to the 370s) turned that standing into reach. A long Sanskrit eulogy carved by his courtier Harisena onto a pillar Ashoka had inscribed six centuries earlier — now inside the fort at Prayagraj — lists kings uprooted in the north, forest chieftains subdued in the centre, and a dozen southern rulers defeated and then pointedly restored to their thrones as tributaries. The distinction matters: the Guptas annexed the north outright and ruled much of the rest through subordinate kings who kept their own courts. Chandragupta II, remembered as Vikramaditya, pushed west against the Saka satraps of Gujarat and Malwa, opening the Arabian Sea ports and, with them, the trade routes to Rome's eastern successors and to Sasanian Iran.

What the empire is remembered for is less the conquering than what the conquering paid for. Gupta gold coinage, minted in astonishing variety, shows kings as archers, lyre-players and lion-slayers. The mathematician Aryabhata, writing at the turn of the sixth century, worked with a place-value system and a strikingly good value for pi; Varahamihira systematised astronomy; the surgical compendium attributed to Sushruta took recognisable shape. Sanskrit drama and poetry, above all Kalidasa's, were composed in or near this milieu. Sculptors at Mathura and Sarnath arrived at an image of the Buddha — downcast eyes, clinging drapery, an inward stillness — that would be copied across South, Southeast and East Asia for a thousand years, while at Udayagiri and elsewhere the free-standing Hindu stone temple began to take its classic form. The rulers themselves were Vaishnava Hindus who nonetheless endowed Buddhist institutions; Kumaragupta I is credited with founding the monastic university at Nalanda. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian, walking through the country around 400 CE, described an orderly, lightly policed realm — though he was a monk describing what he wanted to find, and his account says almost nothing about the peasants who paid for it.

The unravelling came from the northwest. Skandagupta held off Hunnic incursions in the 450s at a cost the treasury seems never to have recovered; by around 500 the Alchon Huns under Toramana and his son Mihirakula had broken through, and although Yashodharman of Malwa and others eventually drove them back in the 520s, they did so as independent powers, not as Gupta servants. The subordinate kingdoms that had always underpinned the structure simply stopped looking to Pataliputra. The last inscriptions of a Gupta claiming imperial titles fall around the middle of the sixth century, and the empire is conventionally closed at 550, though some scholars stretch a rump lineage two or three decades further.
significance: The Gupta centuries fixed a set of forms that outlasted the state by more than a millennium: the Sanskrit literary canon and the courtly patronage that sustained it, the decimal place-value notation that reached Baghdad and then Europe as "Arabic" numerals, the stone temple with its garbhagriha and shikhara, and a Buddha image that became the template from Sri Lanka to Japan. Because so much of what later Indian tradition treats as classical dates from this window, nineteenth- and twentieth-century historians — many of them writing under colonial rule and looking for an indigenous high civilisation to set against it — christened it a golden age, a label that has been sharply contested since. Critics point out that the same era saw the hardening of caste ranking, a narrowing of women's legal position in the law books, and the spread of land grants to Brahmins and temples that some historians read as the beginning of Indian feudalism, and that the prosperity Faxian admired was very unevenly shared. The label persists anyway, which is itself part of the story: the Gupta period is as much a construction of modern Indian self-understanding as it is a chapter of ancient history.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all for the Gupta Empire, so nothing above can be shown on the map — the account is written entirely from reference sources rather than from mapped material. The underlying record is itself thin and skewed: it rests on royal panegyric inscriptions, coin hoards, Puranic king-lists and a handful of foreign travellers, with almost no administrative documents, so regnal dates for even the major emperors vary by a decade or more between scholars, the empire's real degree of central control is genuinely unsettled, and ordinary life — peasants, women, the enslaved — is visible only through prescriptive texts written by the elite.
